record.paper_title: Jet tomography in heavy-ion collisions - Challenges, Results, and Open Problems
record.original_question: Jet tomography in relativistic heavy-ion collisions uses jet quenching: jets produced back-to-back propagate through dense matter and lose energy, with the aim of characterizing properties of the quark-gluon plasma by using the attenuated jets to image the collision interior. How can this method be made into a reliable tomography program, with conclusions that are not misleadingly straightforward, when a heavy-ion collision lacks a controlled flow of penetrating particles, an established dynamical theory of energy loss, and a non-moving, non-fluctuating background medium?

evidence.quote: One of the main challenges is to probe the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) created in such heavy-ion collisions. One set of observables is based on jets, sprays of particles that are produced back-to-back due to the conservation of energy and momentum. Those jets propagate through the dense matter formed while depositing energy. As this jet-energy loss inevitably leads to an attenuation of the jet [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] this concept is referred to as jet quenching.

By studying jet quenching, one should be able to characterize some properties of the medium created. This idea is used e.g. in medicine by x-ray tomography where a beam of particles traverses a medium (e.g. the human body). This beam is deflected and/or absorbed and its remnants are measured in a detector. Finally, this measurement leads to an image of the interior of the human's body. Likewise, one aims to getting an image of the interior of a heavy-ion collision by performing jet tomography.

In contrast to an ideal tomography (for simplicity one might think of an x-ray tomography mentioned above), a heavy-ion collision misses [28] 1. a controlled flow of penetrating particles, 2. an established dynamical theory of the energy loss, 3. and a non-moving, non-fluctuating background medium. Of course, this does not imply that jet tomography cannot be done in heavy-ion collisions but it indicates that conclusions might not be as straightforward as they seem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In a relativistic heavy-ion collision, a dense, rapidly expanding and fluctuating medium (the quark-gluon plasma) is produced. Hard partonic scatterings inside this medium produce pairs of high-energy partons that fragment into collimated sprays of hadrons (jets), approximately back-to-back in the transverse plane by momentum conservation. As these jets traverse the medium they lose energy and are modified, a phenomenon known as jet quenching. The goal of jet tomography is to use the measured attenuation and modification of such jets to reconstruct spatial and dynamical properties of the medium, in analogy with x-ray tomography of a static body by a controlled beam.

Unlike an idealized tomography setup, a heavy-ion collision is characterized by:
(i) the absence of an externally controlled, mono-energetic, penetrating probe beam — the probes are produced internally with a broad spectrum of energies, flavors, and production points sampled by the nuclear overlap geometry;
(ii) the absence of a fully established, first-principles dynamical theory of in-medium parton energy loss valid across all relevant energy scales and coupling regimes; and
(iii) the absence of a static, homogeneous background — the medium expands hydrodynamically, cools, and exhibits event-by-event geometric and quantum fluctuations.

Problem. Formulate a mathematically and physically reliable jet-tomography program for heavy-ion collisions: namely, specify a procedure that, taking as input experimentally measurable jet observables (such as nuclear modification factors, di-jet asymmetries, jet substructure, and azimuthal anisotropies) together with a model of the fluctuating, evolving medium and a model of in-medium energy loss, produces quantitative reconstructions of medium properties (such as the local transport coefficient $\hat{q}(x,t)$, temperature, and density profiles) with controlled and demonstrably non-misleading systematic and statistical uncertainties, in spite of the three obstacles above.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an overarching open research challenge in heavy-ion physics rather than a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture. Active research programs (e.g., JETSCAPE Bayesian analyses) continue to extract medium properties such as $\hat{q}$ from jet data, but a fully reliable tomographic inversion accounting for all three listed obstacles remains an open goal as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: JETSCAPE Collaboration multistage jet quenching Bayesian analysis
status_evidence.snippet: Bayesian model-to-data comparison constrains the jet transport coefficient qhat in QGP, with substantial remaining uncertainties from medium modeling and energy-loss prescriptions.
status_evidence.claim: Tomographic extraction of medium properties from jets is ongoing with significant systematic uncertainties, indicating the program is not yet fully resolved.
